title: VENTOLIN HFA (albuterol sulfate inhalation aerosol), for oral inhalation use: full prescribing information
journal: US Food and Drug Administration, approved prescribing information, initial US approval 1981; DailyMed structured product labelling version 30, published 6 April 2026
funder: GlaxoSmithKline LLC holds the application and submits the labelling text; the US Food and Drug Administration approves it.
result: Indicated for treatment or prevention of bronchospasm in adult and paediatric patients aged 4 years and older with reversible obstructive airway disease, and for prevention of exercise-induced bronchospasm in the same ages; the dose is 2 inhalations every 4 to 6 hours, or 15 to 30 minutes before exercise, and each actuation delivers 108 µg of albuterol sulfate from the mouthpiece, equivalent to 90 µg of albuterol base. Activation of beta2-adrenergic receptors on airway smooth muscle activates adenyl cyclase and raises intracellular cyclic AMP, which activates protein kinase A, which inhibits the phosphorylation of myosin and lowers intracellular ionic calcium concentrations, resulting in relaxation; albuterol relaxes the smooth muscle of all airways from the trachea to the terminal bronchioles and acts as a functional antagonist, relaxing the airway irrespective of the spasmogen; increased cyclic AMP concentrations are also associated with inhibition of release of mediators from mast cells in the airway. Beta2-adrenoceptors comprise 10% to 50% of the total beta-adrenoceptors of the human heart. Systemic levels are low after inhalation of recommended doses: in 12 healthy subjects given 1080 µg of albuterol base, mean peak plasma concentration was approximately 3 ng/ml, time to peak 0.42 hours against 0.17 hours for a CFC-propelled inhaler, and the apparent terminal plasma half-life approximately 4.6 hours. Beta-adrenergic agonists may produce significant hypokalaemia, possibly through intracellular shunting, with potential adverse cardiovascular effects; the decrease in serum potassium is usually transient and does not require supplementation. Hypokalaemia and changes in blood glucose may occur; caution is advised in diabetes mellitus, and large doses of intravenous albuterol have been reported to aggravate pre-existing diabetes mellitus and ketoacidosis. Signs of overdosage include seizures, angina, hypertension or hypotension, tachycardia with rates up to 200 beats/min, arrhythmias, tremor, muscle cramps, hyperglycaemia, hypokalaemia and metabolic acidosis. Fatalities have been reported in association with excessive use of inhaled sympathomimetic drugs in patients with asthma; the exact cause of death is unknown, but cardiac arrest following an unexpected development of a severe acute asthmatic crisis and subsequent hypoxia is suspected. A need for more doses than usual may mark destabilisation of asthma and requires re-evaluation of the patient and the treatment regimen, with special consideration of the possible need for anti-inflammatory treatment; beta-adrenergic agonist bronchodilators alone may not be adequate to control asthma in many patients. Paradoxical bronchospasm may be life threatening and frequently occurs with the first use of a new canister. In 202 adults and adolescents treated with 2 inhalations four times daily for 12 weeks, adverse reactions with an incidence of 3% or more and more common than placebo were throat irritation (10% against 7%), viral respiratory infections (7% against 4%), upper respiratory inflammation (5% against 2%), cough (5% against 2%) and musculoskeletal pain (5% against 4%).
